title: Optical wordlines: photoconductor-gated storage nodes, no access transistor
idea: Reverse the wordline's role from voltage to light: each storage capacitor reaches its bitline through a nanoscale amorphous-selenium/chalcogenide photoconductor (dark resistivity >1e14 ohm-cm), and a row is selected by a ~1 ns light pulse in a SiN waveguide running under it. In the dark the node is isolated by an insulator rather than a leaky transistor.
why: Attacks the access-transistor leakage tail (fact 3) and wordline coupling/voltage (facts 9,10): dark-current-limited retention of seconds (>=30x fewer refreshes), no 3 V electrical wordline swing, and no capacitive row hammer.

title: Inside-out capacitor: block-copolymer pore sponge replaces one tall pillar
idea: Flip the capacitor from a solid pillar into voids: inside each cell footprint a self-assembled block-copolymer template is etched into sacrificial oxide as ~10 nm pores (AR ~20 each), then coated TiN/ZrO2/TiN by ALD, so area comes from many shallow holes instead of one 70:1 pillar.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): ~2-3x electrode area at one third of the aspect ratio, reaching ~5 fF without AR 115 and removing pillar-collapse yield loss.

title: Ion-held charge: solid-electrolyte double-layer cell capacitor
idea: Swap the dielectric's role from a polarizing lattice to mobile ions: a 3-5 nm proton- or Li-conducting solid electrolyte between blocking electrodes piles ions into a ~0.5 nm Helmholtz layer at each plate, giving ~10-20 uF/cm2; ions travel <1 nm, so charging is ns-scale.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): effective k/t ~30x a ZrO2 stack, so a 10:1 cup reaches 5 fF and the 60-75:1 etch disappears; risks are electronic leakage and ion back-relaxation.

title: Vacuum as the insulator: field-emission two-terminal crossbar storage cell
idea: Reverse insulator and conductor: each storage node is a metal island over a sealed 3-5 nm vacuum gap to a sharp emitter at a wordline/bitline crossing; below the Fowler-Nordheim threshold the gap passes essentially nothing, while ~2x the field drives uA emission to charge or discharge it in ns.
why: Leakage tail and 3D blocker (facts 2,3): super-exponential I-V gives >1e12 on/off with no transistor, so 4F2 crossbar tiers can stack with no lateral transistor at all.

title: Reverse the charge wall: 50-electron bits read by single-electron transistors
idea: Instead of fighting for ~30,000 electrons in a 5 fF pillar, store ~50 electrons on a 0.01 fF planar node and move all the gain into the reader: a 3-5 nm room-temperature silicon Coulomb island coupled to the node swings its current by decades per few electrons.
why: Charge wall and capacitor process (facts 1,4): the tall capacitor vanishes (planar ~4F2 cell) and CV2 write energy drops ~100x; risks are RT single-electron uniformity and keeping 50 electrons from leaking.

title: Phase not charge: parametric-oscillator bits sustained by their own pump
idea: Turn refresh from a tax into the storage itself: each bit is a high-Q nanomechanical or LC resonator pumped at 2f by a shared row line, oscillating in one of two phases (0 or pi) that the pump keeps alive; read by phase comparison, write with a brief seed pulse (a modern Goto parametron).
why: Refresh and row hammer (facts 3,9): no static charge to leak or disturb; at Q ~1e4 the shared pump costs ~fW per bit versus 46 fJ/bit refresh; risk is resonator density (~100 nm NEMS).

title: Series negative-capacitance layer that raises cell capacitance
idea: Reverse the series-capacitor rule: add a thin HZO ferroelectric biased into its negative-capacitance branch in series with the ZrO2/Al2O3 cell dielectric, so 1/C = 1/C_DE - 1/|C_FE| and total capacitance rises 2-3x above the dielectric alone while |C_FE| > C_DE keeps it hysteresis-free.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): acts like k ~70+ without new high-k chemistry, giving 5 fF at AR ~30 instead of 75; risk is stabilizing NC with multi-domain films.

title: Read ferroelectric bits by strain, never by switching
idea: Flip FeRAM's read path from electrical to mechanical: each HZO or AlScN ferroelectric capacitor sits on a piezoresistive channel; a small sub-coercive voltage makes up- and down-polarized cells expand or contract (opposite piezo sign), modulating channel resistance, so polarization is read without being switched.
why: Destructive read and fatigue (fact 8): removes the read-switch-restore cycle, cutting read energy ~5-10x and limiting wear to writes only.

title: Imprint as a feature: work-function-biased antiferroelectric bistable cell
idea: Reverse a reliability defect into the design: asymmetric electrodes (~1 eV work-function gap) or a fixed dipole layer around antiferroelectric ZrO2 shift one of its double-hysteresis loops to straddle 0 V, making the AFE bistable at zero bias while keeping AFE's high endurance (no FE domain pinning, target >1e15 cycles).
why: Refresh and voltage floor (facts 3,10): nonvolatile zero-bias storage written at ~1 V by a field-induced transition, removing refresh energy.

title: One heavy-metal strip: forward to write, backward to read
idea: Rearrange the spintronic stack around one effect run both ways: a perpendicular nanomagnet on a Pt or Bi2Se3 strip is written by spin-orbit torque (charge to spin) and read by the inverse, a GHz pulse excites precession whose spin pumping yields an inverse-spin-Hall voltage whose sign is the bit; no MgO tunnel barrier.
why: Endurance and refresh (fact 3): nonvolatile with no barrier to break down, aiming at DRAM-like unlimited cycles; drops the tungsten-heavy MTJ stack; risk is a uV-scale read signal.

title: Strain-held Mott latch: VO2 parked inside its hysteresis window
idea: Reverse the bias logic: a static strain from a piezoelectric underlayer holds a W-doped VO2 nanobar at the middle of its metal-insulator hysteresis, and ns current or voltage pulses flip it metallic or insulating; the electronic phase, not stored charge, holds the bit and reads as ~100x resistance contrast.
why: Refresh and endurance (fact 3): nothing leaks because the state is a thermodynamic phase, and Mott switching moves no atoms (target >1e12 cycles); risks are room-temperature hysteresis width and thermal crosstalk.

title: Telescoping nanotube bit: storage as superlubric shell position
idea: Rearrange the bit into geometry: the inner shell of a double-wall carbon nanotube slides in or out of its outer shell (a wear-free superlubric van der Waals bearing) between two electrostatic detents; in the out position it tunnels to a contact, so read is current on/off and write is a ns electrostatic pull.
why: Refresh and endurance (fact 3): no charge to leak, near-zero-wear sliding aims at unlimited cycles in a ~10 nm footprint; risk is deterministic nanotube placement.

title: The wall is the bit: conducting domain walls in insulating ferroelectric
idea: Rearrange which part stores the data: in LiNbO3 or BiFeO3 films a domain wall conducts while domains insulate; a write creates or erases a wall across a 20 nm electrode gap, and a sub-coercive read senses the wall current without disturbing it.
why: Destructive read and refresh (facts 3,8): nonvolatile NDRO with uA read current and no restore write; 1-2 nm walls make density litho-limited, not charge-limited.

title: The channel is the bit: ferroelectric-semiconductor transistor, no capacitor
idea: Merge storage and access roles into one layer: an alpha-In2Se3-type ferroelectric semiconductor forms the transistor channel itself, and its own polarization bends the band to set high or low current; there is no capacitor and no separate gate ferroelectric to fatigue.
why: Capacitor and 3D blockers (facts 1,2): 1T 4F2 thin-film cell stackable in tiers, nonvolatile so refresh disappears; risk is polarization screening by channel carriers.

title: The wire is the memory: electron-position cells that store and route
idea: Erase the line between storage and interconnect: four-dot silicon dangling-bond or molecular cells hold a bit as which diagonal two electrons occupy, and the same cells chained in a line shift the bit to the array edge under a clocked field (quantum-dot cellular automata); no bitlines, no charge sharing.
why: Data movement and periphery (facts 5,7): moving a bit costs near-kT energy instead of pJ, cells are ~2 nm; risks are room-temperature margins and single defects breaking chains.

title: Access transistor turns avalanche amplifier during the read window
idea: Reverse the access device's job on read: for a 1 ns window its drain junction is biased just above breakdown, so the few hundred electrons released from a tiny 0.1 fF node trigger quenched impact-ionization gain of ~100 (SPAD-like) and produce a full-swing bitline signal; at idle it is a normal off transistor.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): Cs can shrink ~50x to a planar capacitor while keeping sense margin; risks are avalanche noise, dark counts and hot-carrier wear.

title: Molecular spin-state bit: hysteretic Fe(II) spin-crossover film
idea: Instead of moving electrons in and out of a node, flip their pairing inside an ion: a thin film of a room-temperature-hysteretic Fe(II) spin-crossover complex toggles between low-spin and high-spin with ~10-20% dielectric-constant change; a field/charge pulse sets the state and a capacitive divider reads it.
why: Refresh (fact 3): a bistable molecular state needs no refresh and molecule-scale units (~2 nm) promise density; risks are solid-film switching speed and cycling.

title: A magnet with no magnetization: Mn3Sn Weyl antiferromagnet bits
idea: Reverse ferromagnet thinking: store the bit in the chiral spin order of a noncollinear antiferromagnet (Mn3Sn) with ~zero net moment, toggled by spin-orbit torque and read through its large Berry-curvature anomalous Hall voltage rather than through magnetization.
why: Density, speed and refresh (fact 3): zero stray field lets cells pack below 20 nm pitch without coupling, ps-scale dynamics, nonvolatile; risk is small Hall signal at tiny sizes.

title: Remove defects, not add capacitance: hBN-sealed 2D gain cell
idea: Reverse retention strategy from bigger capacitor to zero trap states: a WSe2 or MoS2 monolayer write transistor fully encapsulated in hBN (no dangling bonds) charges an hBN-isolated graphene storage gate, so the trap-assisted tunneling behind the 13 fA leakage tail has no sites to use.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): 1.5-2 eV-gap channels with clean interfaces target <1e-19 A, i.e., minutes-to-hours retention and >100x less refresh energy; thin-film tiers stack (fact 2).

title: Mechanical access: NEMS relay air gap isolates every cell
idea: Swap electronic isolation for a physical gap: each capacitor reaches its bitline through a nanoscale electrostatic TiN or carbon cantilever relay (5 nm gap) that closes only when the wordline pulls it; open, the leakage is literally zero, and the relay needs no doped silicon so it builds in the BEOL.
why: Leakage tail and 3D (facts 2,3): retention set only by the capacitor dielectric (hours) and BEOL-stackable cells; risk is contact wear capping endurance near 1e10-1e12.

title: Sliding ferroelectric bits: polarization set by atomic-layer registry
idea: Flip the direction of motion: in bilayer hBN or 3R-MoS2, sliding one layer in-plane by one bond length reverses the out-of-plane polarization (AB to BA stacking); write with a vertical field pulse, read by tunnel-current asymmetry, with no ion displacement or oxygen vacancies to fatigue.
why: Endurance and density: sliding ferroelectrics switch essentially fatigue-free in 0.6 nm films, enabling nonvolatile no-refresh cells stacked by layer transfer; risk is wafer-scale stacking-order control.

title: Cold capacitor: quantum paraelectric k~1000 at liquid-nitrogen temperature
idea: Reverse the operating environment: run the array at 77 K, where SrTiO3 or KTaO3 films reach k ~500-2000 and silicon leakage collapses, so the cell capacitor becomes planar or a shallow 5:1 cup, with the memory sharing the accelerator's liquid-nitrogen loop.
why: Charge wall and capital (facts 1,4): 5 fF without the high-AR etch, leakage down >1e6 so refresh effectively vanishes; LN2 cost offset by lower wire resistance.

title: Grow, don't etch: VLS nanowire electrodes at 150:1 aspect ratio
idea: Reverse subtractive to additive: Al or Sn catalyst dots on each storage node grow vertical silicon nanowire electrodes by vapor-liquid-solid growth (150:1 is easy to grow and impossible to etch), then ALD high-k and a conformal top electrode wrap them.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): the AR ~115 needed for more charge is reached without aspect-ratio-dependent etch limits, ~8 fF per cell; risk is catalyst contamination and wire placement.

title: Store the absence: deep-depletion SiC capacitors hold bits for years
idea: Reverse what the bit is: a 4H-SiC MOS capacitor pulsed into deep depletion stores '1' as a missing inversion layer; with a 3.26 eV gap, thermal generation is ~1e18 slower than silicon, so the empty state lasts years at room temperature. Built on 150 mm SiC power lines with 0.5-1 um steppers.
why: Refresh (fact 3) eliminated, U.S. manufacturability (SiC fabs exist domestically); ~1 um2 cells, so first market is refresh-free, hot or rad-hard memory tiers.

title: Vertical CCD pillars: bits climb a 100-gate stack instead of being addressed
idea: Reverse addressing: rather than moving the sense amp to the bit, clock charge packets up and down a 180 nm channel hole lined with polysilicon through 100 LPCVD-deposited gate layers (hole etched with 1990s deep-trench AR ~40); a sense node at the pillar top reads packets in sequence, ~50 bits per pillar.
why: Litho/capital (fact 4): one 180 nm mask defines holes while film thickness sets vertical pitch, ~0.003 um2/bit footprint (near 12 nm DRAM) with zero EUV; ~50 ns average shift latency; risk is transfer efficiency in poly channels.

title: Core memory reborn: electroplated permalloy nano-toroid stacks
idea: Swap charge for flux: plate 1 um permalloy rings around through-mask copper posts (1990s thin-film-head plating) in 20 tiers, select by coincident X/Y half-currents and sense on a shared winding, a destructive read like DRAM but with zero leakage and unlimited endurance.
why: Refresh and standby power (fact 3), U.S. manufacturability via disk-head plating know-how; ~0.05 um2/bit across 20 tiers (still ~60x DRAM area), aimed at refresh-free persistent buffers.

title: Lay the capacitor down: MLCC-style 30-electrode stacks inside each cell
idea: Rearrange from tall-and-thin to flat-and-many: deposit 30 alternating TiN/Nb2O5 layers, pattern 180 nm cells with two offset staircase edge contacts so odd and even electrodes interleave like a ceramic MLCC; capacitance comes from layer count, not etch depth or litho.
why: Charge wall (fact 1) at 180 nm: 0.2 um2 x 30 layers x ~40 fF/um2 ~ 240 fF per cell, enough for 4-bit multilevel storage, EUV-free (fact 4); risk is film stress and staircase contact yield.

title: Run the image-sensor pixel backward: pinned-photodiode memory lines
idea: Convert depreciated 180-110 nm CMOS image-sensor lines into memory by reversing the pixel: inject charge into each pinned photodiode from the floating diffusion (fill-and-spill), hold it in the pinned well (dark current ~1-10 e-/s), then transfer forward and read by correlated double sampling with column ADCs; 3000 e- full well and 2 e- noise allow ~6 bits per cell.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and capital: retention of seconds instead of 64 ms, capacity from existing paid-off fabs; ~0.2 um2/bit effective, so a refresh-light warm tier sold on fab-conversion economics.

title: Leakage as the keeper: Si/SiGe tunnel-diode latched storage node
idea: Reverse leakage from enemy to holder: two series Si/SiGe resonant interband tunnel diodes (1990s low-temperature CVD) on a 180 nm cell's storage node cross their negative-resistance curves at two stable points, so tiny diode currents continuously restore '0' or '1' against junction leakage; one access FET reads and writes (tunneling SRAM).
why: Refresh (fact 3): static retention in a ~2-device footprint with pW-scale valley-current standby; no capacitor needed; risk is peak-to-valley ratio uniformity.

title: Capacitor first, transistor last: bonded perovskite capacitor wafer
idea: Reverse fabrication order: build a planar BST/SrTiO3 capacitor array first and crystallize it at 700 C (k ~300, the 1990s gigabit-DRAM dielectric), then smart-cut bond (1995) a pre-implanted thin silicon layer on top and finish 180 nm access transistors below 450 C so the perovskite never sees transistor hazards.
why: Charge wall and capital (facts 1,4): planar 0.2 um2 x ~100 fF/um2 ~ 20 fF with no deep etch; tiers repeat by further bonds; risk is hydrogen damage to the perovskite and bond overlay.

title: Read by emptying with a spoon: charge-metering multilevel readout
idea: Reverse sensing from measuring a level to counting scoops: a ~100 fF 180 nm cell stores one of 16 charge levels; readout clocks the charge through a CCD-style metering gate that skims fixed ~6 fC packets onto the bitline while a counter tallies packets until empty, a 4-bit value without an analog ADC.
why: Density at relaxed litho (fact 4): 4 bits/cell cuts the ~225x area penalty of 180 nm to ~56x before tiering, on depreciated tools; risk is metering accuracy and ~16-clock read time.

title: Latch-up as a feature: gated vertical thyristor bit
idea: Turn CMOS's classic failure into the storage mechanism: a vertical p-n-p-n stack in 1990s bulk silicon, 180 nm litho, with a capacitively coupled gate on its p-base latches into high-current on (1) or stays blocking (0); gate pulses set and reset it, and the read current is uA-scale with no capacitor.
why: Charge wall and sense signal (facts 1,8): no capacitor, read signal ~100x a DRAM cell, ~8F2 footprint; standby holding current or periodic refresh is the trade.

title: Let the electrode become the dielectric: anodized metal-sponge capacitors
idea: Reverse deposition: oblique-sputter a porous aluminum or niobium sponge into each 180 nm cell, then anodize it so the metal converts itself into conformal Al2O3 or Nb2O5 (k ~41) that self-limits at ~2 nm per volt even inside hidden pores; fill with CVD TiN as the counter electrode, like an electrolytic capacitor.
why: Charge wall (fact 1) with a wet 1900s-era process: ~10-30x surface gain per footprint, no ALD or EUV, abundant Al/Nb; risk is anodic oxide leakage and pore filling.

title: Store the bit as a shape: snap-through buckled polysilicon beams
idea: Rearrange storage from charge to geometry: a compressively stressed 2 um polysilicon micro-bridge (1990s surface micromachining) buckles up or down; electrodes above and below snap it between states in ~50-100 ns and a capacitive pickoff reads the gap, with no contact so no stiction or wear.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and rad-hardness: zero-leakage nonvolatile storage with contactless (fatigue-limited only) cycling; ~4 um2/bit, so it targets harsh-environment and refresh-free buffers.

title: Persistent current instead of leaky charge: niobium flux-loop memory
idea: Reverse decay into perpetuity: each bit is a single flux quantum circulating in a superconducting niobium loop built with the 1990s Nb/AlOx/Nb trilayer process (1-2 um junctions) at 4 K, where current flows forever without refresh; a Josephson junction switches on read depending on loop current.
why: Energy (facts 3,5): ~1e-19 J switching and zero static loss, the natural partner for cryogenic accelerators; density is poor (~10 um2/bit), so the gain is energy, not cost.

title: Cold old node: 77 K planar-capacitor DRAM at 180 nm
idea: Reverse the scaling logic: run a 180 nm 1T1C array whose storage element is only a planar MOS capacitor (no trench, no stack) at liquid-nitrogen temperature, where junction and subthreshold leakage fall >1e6, so a 2 fF planar cap holds data for hours while the transistors gain mobility and steeper slope.
why: Capital and refresh (facts 3,4): a few-mask cell on depreciated tools with refresh gone; risk is shifting cost into system cooling.

title: Rotate the array into depth: four capacitors stacked in one trench
idea: Rearrange the 2D array vertically: in a 1990s-style 0.25 um wide, 10 um deep trench, deposit alternating doped-poly electrodes and collar oxides to form four isolated storage capacitors stacked along the trench, each reached by its own buried strap and sidewall transistor at a different depth (depth-addressed wordlines).
why: Density without a litho shrink (fact 4): four cells per trench footprint, ~25 fF each (2 um2 of 5 nm ONO per segment); risk is forming straps and transistors at depth.

title: Make flash leak on purpose: direct-tunnel nanocrystal storage
idea: Reverse flash's priorities: grow silicon nanocrystals on a 2 nm tunnel oxide in a 180 nm logic flow (Tiwari-style, 1996) so electrons enter and leave by direct tunneling in ~10-100 ns at +/-2-3 V with no Fowler-Nordheim damage, trading retention (seconds to hours) for near-unlimited endurance; the bit is a threshold shift read non-destructively.
why: Refresh and destructive read (facts 3,8): 1T capacitor-free cell with >=1000x DRAM retention and NDRO; risk is Vt window and endurance beyond 1e12.

title: Capacitor that shrinks on read: gated-diode voltage amplification
idea: Reverse the capacitor's role mid-operation: a 180 nm gated diode stores charge in its inversion layer; on read the gate is raised so capacitance collapses from Cox to Cdep, pushing the charge out as a 3-5x larger bitline voltage swing, built-in gain without a sense transistor.
why: Charge wall and periphery (facts 1,7,8): 3-5x less stored charge for the same signal, enabling planar storage, longer bitlines and fewer sense amps.

title: Crucible-free memory: laser-crystallized silicon gain cells on glass
idea: Reverse the substrate dependency: deposit amorphous silicon on glass or metal-foil panels and excimer-laser-crystallize it (1990s LTPS display process, >=1 um rules) into 2T gain cells, so the storage tier needs no Czochralski ingot, no high-purity quartz crucible and no 300 mm wafer.
why: Scarce resource (Spruce Pine quartz >80%) and capital: capacity from display-class lines priced per m2, though LTPS leakage needs ~10 ms refresh; a bulk-capacity tier strategy.

title: One contact for eight bits: NAND-chained capacitor strings
idea: Rearrange cells from parallel to series: chain eight 180 nm 1T1C cells with one bitline contact (as in early-1990s NAND-structured DRAM proposals), read them destructively in fixed order from the contact end and write back in reverse order, so contacts no longer set cell area.
why: Density and periphery (facts 4,7): cell area falls toward 4F2 as seven of eight contacts vanish; sequential access suits page-streaming AI workloads; risk is far-cell latency.

title: Polarization-built well: GaN 2DEG pocket holds charge for hours
idea: Reverse doping-defined wells for polarization-defined ones: in AlGaN/GaN the built-in polarization makes an electron well with no dopants; a gated, isolated 2DEG pocket stores electrons behind a 3.4 eV-gap barrier and an adjacent HEMT channel senses it, using 0.25-0.5 um GaN RF fab tools.
why: Leakage (fact 3) and U.S. manufacturability: wide gap and epitaxial barriers target hours of retention in existing U.S. defense GaN fabs; risk is trap-driven charge drift (current collapse).

title: Light-latched bits: self-electro-optic effect device memory planes
idea: Reverse light's role from signal to holder: arrays of symmetric SEEDs (GaAs quantum-well p-i-n pairs, 1990s Bell Labs, ~5 um pixels) latch a bit through photocurrent feedback under a uniform bias beam; pages are written and read by light in parallel with no electrical wires.
why: Data movement (fact 5): page-parallel optical I/O at fJ/bit and static retention while illuminated; low density (~25 um2/bit) fits optically linked buffers, not bulk capacity.

title: Ferroelectric as backup, not primary: dual-mode DRAM/FeRAM capacitor
idea: Reverse the ferroelectric's role: run a PZT or SBT capacitor (1990s FeRAM process, 0.35-0.18 um) as a plain DRAM cell below its coercive voltage during active use, and switch polarization only to park a row when it goes idle, so idle rows need no refresh at all.
why: Refresh power (fact 3): idle rows draw zero refresh while active rows keep DRAM endurance; polarization switches only once per idle event (~1e9 lifetime); ready for old-node fabs.

title: A battery per bit: LiPON nano-cell stores the bit as voltage
idea: Swap stored charge for stored chemistry: each 180 nm-patterned cell is a ~50 nm-thick LiCoO2/LiPON/Si thin-film battery (LiPON: Oak Ridge, 1992) whose state of charge is the bit, read non-destructively as open-circuit voltage by a high-impedance FET; self-discharge, not junction leakage, sets retention.
why: Refresh and destructive read (facts 3,8): months of retention, no charge sharing, multilevel via voltage plateaus; risks are Li diffusion speed for ~100 ns writes and intercalation endurance.

title: Voltage strains a magnet: PZT-Galfenol magnetoelectric bit
idea: Reverse magnetics' write path from current to voltage: a 180 nm elliptical Galfenol (FeGa, U.S. Navy 1998, rare-earth-free) nanomagnet on a PZT film is strained by a ~1 V pulse that rotates its easy axis and toggles magnetization, read non-destructively by a GMR stack.
why: Write energy and refresh (facts 3,10): ~fJ current-free writes, nonvolatile, all from 1990s sputtering, PZT and GMR-head processes with no rare earths; risk is deterministic 180-degree switching.
